cards.text: This is Jeremiah, the LORD's prophet, and the LORD is sending him on an errand. Step one: go buy a clay jar from a potter. As a guy who once got picked up for a quarter at a going-out-of-business sale, I LOVE a story that starts with shopping.

cards.question: Jeremiah isn't making this trip with his clay jar alone. Who does the LORD tell him to take along?

answers.text: Some elders and leaders of the priests
His scribe and a few servants
The king and his royal officials

cards.text: Then the LORD tells Jeremiah to go out to the Valley of Ben-hinnom, near the entrance of the Potsherd Gate, and proclaim His words there. A brand new clay jar headed for the Potsherd Gate, friend, and I've got a feeling this jar does NOT make the sequel.

cards.question: The message Jeremiah proclaims in the Valley of Ben-hinnom is for the kings of ___ and the residents of Jerusalem.

cards.text: The LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says He's going to bring such disaster on this place that the ears of all who hear of it will ring. Friend, that is not a little notification ding.

cards.question: Why does the LORD say He's bringing this disaster on the people of Judah and Jerusalem?

answers.text: They abandoned Him for other gods
They lost a battle to Egypt
They broke a treaty with Babylon

cards.question: The LORD says the gods the people burned incense to were gods their fathers and the kings of Judah had known for generations.

cards.text: They've made this a foreign place and filled it with the blood of the innocent. They built high places to Baal, to burn their children in the fire as offerings to Baal.

cards.question: The LORD says burning children as offerings to Baal is something He never commanded, and it never even entered His mind.

cards.text: So the days are coming, the LORD says, when this place won't be called Topheth or the Valley of Ben-hinnom anymore. It's getting a new name, and friend, it is not a nicer one.

cards.question: The LORD says Topheth, the Valley of Ben-hinnom, will be called the Valley of ___.

cards.text: Back in Jeremiah 18:12 the people said they'd follow their own plans, and now the LORD says that in this place He'll ruin the plans of Judah and Jerusalem. They'll fall by the sword before their enemies, and their carcasses will be food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth.

cards.question: The LORD says He'll make Jerusalem a desolation and an object of scorn. How will the people passing by react?

answers.text: Be appalled and scoff at her wounds
Stop and help bind up her wounds
Mourn for her and bring her gifts

cards.text: Friend, I'm not cracking a single joke here, because this is as heavy as it gets. In the siege and distress their enemies bring on them, the LORD says they'll eat the flesh of their own sons and daughters, and one another's flesh too.
Now, the jar, and I called it, friend: right in front of the men who came along, the LORD tells Jeremiah to shatter it.

cards.question: In Jeremiah 18:4 the potter formed a flawed vessel into another one. But what does the LORD say about the shattered potter's jar He compares this nation and city to?

answers.text: It can never again be repaired
A better jar will replace it

cards.question: The LORD says they will bury the dead in ___ until there is no more room to bury them.

cards.text: This is what the LORD will do to this place and its residents: He'll make the city like Topheth. Even the houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah will be defiled like that place.

cards.question: The LORD says the houses of Jerusalem will be defiled like Topheth. What did people do on the rooftops of those houses?

answers.text: Burned incense to all the host of heaven
Kept watch for the enemy's armies
Prayed toward the house of the LORD

cards.text: Then Jeremiah returns from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy. And he carries the message somewhere a whole lot of people can hear it.

cards.question: After coming back from Topheth, where does Jeremiah stand to proclaim the LORD's message?

answers.text: The courtyard of the house of the LORD
The palace of the king of Judah

cards.text: And this time it isn't just the elders and the priests who hear it. He proclaims it to ALL the people, which is like going from the six-person group chat straight to reply-all.

The LORD of Hosts says He's about to bring every disaster He has pronounced, because they have stiffened their necks so as not to heed His words. Not the stiff neck you get from falling asleep on the couch, friend, but the kind where you hear every word and STILL won't turn your head.

cards.question: The LORD says the disaster He pronounced will come on Jerusalem and on all the villages around it.

findings.problem: The joke only works if the baker already knows that 'potsherd' means a broken piece of pottery. Most adults don't, so the line 'this jar does NOT make the sequel' won't land without an explanation, and the card has no room to give one.

rule.text: It clicks instantly for any adult, with no explaining.

findings.problem: The right answer 'Slaughter' is a common noun, while the wrong answers 'Elah' and 'Jezreel' are proper place names. The answers aren't the same kind of thing. Card 10's setup, 'it is not a nicer one,' also points straight to the only grim-sounding option, so the right answer stands out and the wrong answers are ruled out.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The card says 'Back in Jeremiah 18:12 the people said they'd follow their own plans.' In the BSB, Jeremiah 18:12 is the LORD saying what they will reply ('But they will reply...'), not a report of something the people said. The card also puts 18:12 next to 19:7 as cause and effect, a link Jeremiah 19:7 doesn't state.

rule.text: When he connects two passages, or explains what a law was for, he says only what the texts state.

findings.problem: The card packs too many beats into one story card: the 18:12 callback, the LORD ruining their plans, falling by the sword, and carcasses fed to birds and beasts.

rule.text: Aim for one beat per story card. Two is the most. If a story card has more than two things happening, split it.

findings.problem: The question first says the potter in 18:4 reshaped a flawed vessel, then asks 'But what does the LORD say...'. The 'But' rules out the wrong answer 'The potter can reshape it' and leans against 'A better jar will replace it,' so the setup gives the answer away.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The card is a flat paraphrase of verses 12 and 13 with none of Papa Dorin's voice. The moment could carry his personality without muddying a fact.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: The comparison 'going from the six-person group chat straight to reply-all' blends two images: a group chat and an email reply-all. It also doesn't show a small audience growing into everyone, because reply-all goes back to the same group. A stranger would say 'huh?'. The 'six-person' count can also be misread as the number of elders and priests, which the text never gives.

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: Stop 1 card 12 and stop 2 card 2 build their content on Jeremiah 18, the previous passage. The docs say that passage is provided 'for context only. It is not part of the lesson,' but they also allow facts from outside the passage when they help, with a reference.
findings.question: May Prep cards quote or call back to the previous passage (here, Jeremiah 18:4 and 18:12) to set up a contrast or question, or should the previous passage be used only as background for the writer and never appear on a card?
